whatItIs.title: What it is
whatItIs.wide: The lowest part of the cerebellum, the tonsils, extends below the foramen magnum, the opening at the base of the skull. The cerebellum helps control balance and coordination. It's often linked to a lower back part of the skull that is smaller or shaped differently than usual, which crowds the brain. Less often, it develops later in life for other reasons.
whatItIs.narrow: The lowest part of the cerebellum, the tonsils, extends below the opening at the base of the skull. It's often linked to a lower back part of the skull that is smaller or shaped differently than usual, which crowds the brain. Less often, it develops later in life for other reasons.

whoHasIt.title: Who has it
whoHasIt.wide: Most people are born with the skull differences that lead to it. Some never have symptoms; others first notice them as teens or adults.
whoHasIt.narrow: Most people are born with the skull differences that lead to it. Some never have symptoms; others first notice them as teens or adults.

howFound.title: How it's found
howFound.wide: Usually with an MRI scan and a doctor's exam, sometimes by chance during a scan for something else. A doctor looks at the scan together with your symptoms.
howFound.narrow: Usually with an MRI scan and a doctor's exam, sometimes by chance.

feel.title: What it can feel like
feel.intro: Chiari looks different for everyone, and many people with Type I have no symptoms at all.

classic.wide: The classic sign is a headache at the back of the head that comes on after coughing, sneezing or straining.
classic.narrow: The classic sign is a headache at the back of the head after coughing, sneezing or straining.

symptoms.wide: Numbness or tingling in the hands and feet
symptoms.narrow: Numbness or tingling in hands and feet

symptoms.wide: Weakness or trouble with fine hand movements
symptoms.narrow: Weakness or trouble with fine hand movements

symptoms.wide: Breathing or sleep problems, such as sleep apnea
A curve in the spine (scoliosis), especially in children

feel.noSymptoms: Many people with Type I have no symptoms at all.

items.wide: Chiari is a structural difference that can affect balance, nerves and the flow of spinal fluid, not only headaches.
items.narrow: It can affect balance, nerves and the flow of spinal fluid too.

items.wide: Doctors traditionally use about 5 mm below the opening as a cutoff. How far the tonsils extend doesn't always match how someone feels. Some people with a clear descent have no symptoms, and some with less than 5 mm do. Doctors also look at the shape of the tonsils, spinal fluid flow, and whether a syrinx is present.
items.narrow: How far the tonsils extend doesn't always match how someone feels. Doctors also look at tonsil shape, fluid flow, and whether a syrinx is present.

explorer.title: 3D Explorer

typical.label: Typical anatomy
typical.note: The tonsils usually sit at or above the dashed line across the skull opening (a few millimeters below can still be normal), and spinal fluid moves freely around them.
typical.noteShort: Tonsils usually sit at or above the skull opening (a few millimeters below can be normal); fluid moves freely.

chiari.label: Chiari I
chiari.note: The tonsils extend below the opening, at least about 5 mm by the usual definition. In one study of 160 people with Chiari I, the average was about 12 mm, but it ranged from 5 to 25 mm, and the number alone doesn't decide who needs surgery. They are often pointed rather than rounded. The fluid space behind them is often crowded, and in many people fluid flow slows or is blocked there.
chiari.noteShort: Tonsils extend below the opening and often crowd the fluid space; in many people flow slows there.

syrinx.label: Chiari I with syrinx
syrinx.note: A syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity inside the spinal cord. It often develops alongside Chiari, most often in the neck part of the spinal cord.
syrinx.noteShort: A fluid-filled cavity has formed inside the spinal cord.

surgery.label: After decompression
surgery.note: Surgeons remove a small piece of bone at the back of the skull opening and often the back of the first vertebra. Often they also open and patch the brain's covering to make more room for spinal fluid. The tonsils often rise only partly. Surgery improves or stabilizes symptoms in most people, though damage that has already happened may not fully reverse, and some people need more than one operation. Results vary, and surgery isn't right for everyone.
surgery.noteShort: Bone is removed at the back of the opening to make room. Most people improve or stabilize, but results vary, some need another operation, and surgery isn't right for everyone.

explorer.partsButton: Parts list · tap a part in the model

parts.name: Cerebrum
parts.text: The largest part of the brain, responsible for thinking, movement and the senses.

parts.name: Corpus callosum
parts.text: A thick band of nerve fibers connecting the left and right halves of the brain.

parts.name: Cerebellum
parts.text: The back part of the brain that helps control balance and coordination.

parts.name: Fourth ventricle
parts.text: A small fluid-filled space between the brainstem and cerebellum, where spinal fluid passes through.

parts.name: Brainstem
parts.text: Connects the brain to the spinal cord and runs automatic functions like breathing, heart rate and swallowing.

parts.name: Cerebellar tonsil
parts.text: The two lowest parts of the cerebellum. In Chiari, they extend below the opening at the base of the skull and are often pointed (peg-shaped) rather than rounded. They really sit just to either side of the midline and often descend unevenly; the model shows them at their lowest point, where MRI measures them.

parts.name: Foramen magnum
parts.text: The opening at the base of the skull where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.

parts.name: Spinal cord
parts.text: Carries signals between the brain and the rest of the body.

parts.name: Spinal fluid (CSF)
parts.text: Cerebrospinal fluid: clear fluid that cushions the brain and spinal cord. With each heartbeat it pulses back and forth between the skull and the spinal canal.

parts.name: C2 vertebra
parts.text: The second bone of the neck. Its upward peg, the dens, sits just in front of the spinal cord.

parts.name: Syrinx
parts.text: A fluid-filled cavity inside the spinal cord. It often develops alongside Chiari, most often in the neck part of the spinal cord.

parts.name: Bone removed
parts.text: Surgeons remove a small piece of bone at the back of the skull opening and often the back of the first vertebra.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.short: The short version: Open Chiari doesn't know who you are, doesn't use cookies, and never collects health information.

counted.before: To show the totals on the
counted.after: , the site counts visits and a few actions: opening the 3D model, making an Explain It link, and opening a study listing. Counting uses Open Chiari's own counter, which uses no cookies and doesn't build a profile of you. Your browser sends only the name of the action, and the counter adds 1 to a total. It doesn't keep your address, device, browser, country, the page you came from, or the link. When the 3D model is shown on another website, that website's address is noted, so the Impact page can count the sites that use it.

never.text: No accounts, sign-ins, names or email addresses.
Your note goes in the message you send, not in the link. The link holds only the chosen view, after the #. Browsers don't send that part to our server, and the counter never receives it.
Built and printed entirely in your browser. Nothing you tick or type leaves your device.
The "Near" box on Research studies sorts the list on your device and is never sent.

privacy.saved: Calm mode and your language choice are remembered in your own browser so they stay on next time. Clearing your browser data removes them. They're never sent to the site.

outside.text: Cloudflare Pages, which handles the site's traffic like any web host.
served from Open Chiari itself, not from Google or other companies.
collected from ClinicalTrials.gov, run by the U.S. National Library of Medicine, once a day by the site, so your browser never contacts them.
donate pages, study listings and other sites have their own privacy policies.

email.after: , your message is used only to reply and isn't shared. Please don't include medical details.

privacy.changes: If this policy changes, the date at the top changes too, and anything significant is noted on the home page for 30 days.

steps.title: Meet the model
steps.text: This view is cut down the middle of the head and neck. The cerebellum helps control balance and coordination. The foramen magnum is the opening at the base of the skull where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.

steps.title: Typical anatomy
steps.text: The tonsils usually sit at or above the dashed line across the skull opening (a few millimeters below can still be normal), and spinal fluid moves freely around them.

steps.title: The tonsils sit too low
steps.text: The dashed line runs across the opening at the base of the skull. In Chiari, the tonsils, the lowest part of the cerebellum, extend below it, shown by the blue bracket.

steps.title: How fluid flows
steps.text: Cerebrospinal fluid is clear fluid that cushions the brain and spinal cord. With each heartbeat it pulses back and forth between the skull and the spinal canal. In Chiari, the tonsils extend below the line (blue bracket) and fill the space where fluid should pass. Red marks show where flow is often restricted.

steps.title: A syrinx
steps.text: A syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity inside the spinal cord. It often develops alongside Chiari, most often in the neck part of the spinal cord.
